summary: Defines a MIME content type that a mail program or gateway can use to report what happened to a message after it was delivered, such as whether it was displayed. These message disposition notifications work like read receipts. It was replaced by RFC 3798.

plainLanguage.summary: Like asking the post office to tell you when your letter was opened. This memo defines the special email reply that says what happened to your message.

questions: what is a message disposition notification
how do email read receipts work
subtitle: A standard format for email read receipts and delivery confirmations.

tldr.problem: Email senders want to know what happened to a message after it was delivered: Was it read? Printed? Deleted? Different email systems had different ways to do this, making it hard to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2298 defines a MIME content type, message/disposition-notification, that reports on message delivery and display, plus headers that senders can use to request these notifications. It includes fields for the reporting user agent, the original recipient address, the final recipient, and the action taken.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 3798, which refined the format and semantics, but it established the basic framework that most email systems use for read receipts.

today: RFC 2298 was replaced by RFC 3798, which clarifies the format and improves security. Most modern email clients support MDNs (called read receipts, delivery notifications, or read reports), though support for the optional header fields varies. The standard remains important for interoperability, especially in enterprise and gateway environments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Message Disposition Notification (MDN) is an automated email reply that tells the original sender what happened to a message after it was successfully delivered. Examples include the message being displayed to a user, printed, forwarded, deleted without being read, or processed by an automated system.

The RFC defines two things: (1) a MIME content type called message/disposition-notification that carries the notification itself, and (2) three email headers that a sender can include in an original message to request MDNs. This is the standard that puts read receipts on an interoperable footing across different email systems.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like putting a return postcard inside a mailed letter that says please let me know when you get this and what you do with it.

sections.title: What Notifications Can Report
sections.content:
An MDN can report several different outcomes. Displayed means the message was shown to a user in the mail program (though it does not prove the user actually read it). Dispatched> means the message was sent somewhere, like being forwarded, printed, or faxed. Processed> means an automated system handled the message according to rules, such as a mail filter or auto-responder.

Deleted> means the recipient removed the message. Denied> means the recipient refused to send a notification, or the mail system does not support them. Failed> means the notification could not be generated, usually due to an error or unsupported feature. Each notification also includes information about whether the action was manual (done by the user) or automatic (done by the system).
sections.plainLanguage: The notification can say the message was displayed (opened), forwarded, deleted, or that there was a problem sending the notification back.

sections.title: Requesting Notifications
sections.content:
A sender requests MDNs by including a Disposition-Notification-To header in the original message, listing the email address where the notification should be sent. The RFC also defines an Original-Recipient header to preserve the original recipient address in case the message is forwarded, and a Disposition-Notification-Options header for future extensions.

However, requesting a notification is just a request: mail clients are free to ignore it. In fact, the RFC strongly recommends that the mail client ask the user before automatically sending an MDN, to prevent mail loops and privacy violations. If the Disposition-Notification-To address differs from the Return-Path address (the address that appears in the From line), the client should not send the notification automatically without user consent.
sections.plainLanguage: You put a header in your email that says send me a notification to this address, but the recipient's email program might ask them first before actually sending it.

sections.title: Structure of a Notification
sections.content:
An MDN is sent as a MIME multipart/report message with report-type disposition-notification. The first part is a human-readable explanation of what happened. The second part is the machine-readable message/disposition-notification content, which consists of several header-like fields: Reporting-UA (the software that generated the notification), Original-Recipient (from the original message), Final-Recipient (the address where the notification is being generated), and Disposition (describing the action and mode).

Optional fields include MDN-Gateway (if the notification was translated from a foreign email system), Original-Message-ID (to correlate with the original message), and Failure, Error, or Warning fields for additional details if something went wrong. The notification may optionally include the original message or a copy of its headers for reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The notification is a special email made of two parts: a friendly explanation for humans, and a structured report for computers to read automatically.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The biggest concern is that MDNs could be used to confirm a sender's email address is active or that a message was delivered, enabling spam and phishing attacks. To mitigate this, the RFC requires that MDNs MUST NOT be generated in response to other MDNs (to prevent loops), and that a mail client SHOULD obtain user consent before sending any notification, especially if the notification request came from an unexpected address.

Another risk is that an encrypted message should only be returned in its original encrypted form, never decrypted. Senders can also use the failure disposition to send a denied notification instead of confirming delivery. The recommendation is for mail clients to be conservative and let the user decide whether to allow MDN requests, rather than enabling them by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Be careful: confirming that a message was delivered could help spammers and hackers. Always ask the user before sending a notification, never decrypt encrypted messages, and avoid creating mail loops.

sections.title: Gateways and Interoperability
sections.content:
The RFC was designed to work in environments where email passes through gateways between the Internet and other messaging systems like X.400. A gateway can translate a foreign notification (from a non-Internet system) into the standard MDN format, and include an MDN-Gateway field to indicate where the translation happened.

This allows notifications from proprietary systems to be tunneled through Internet Mail and back into the original system, or to a third messaging system. The gateway can preserve foreign addresses and insert simulated RFC 822 headers to maintain compatibility, even if the original notification format was different.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message goes through a bridge to another email system, that bridge can convert that system's read receipts into standard MDN format so they work on the Internet too.
